title: Many seasons, one sun
hookLine: seconds, hours, days and seasons are many, but the sun is one (Asa M1, ang 12)

cards: Open the calendar on your phone. Seconds tick into minutes, minutes into hours. There's a Monday and a Thursday, a March and a November, a summer that feels nothing like winter.
Some days feel like they belong to a different life. And yet every one of those units is measured by the same thing: the sun coming up, going down, the earth tilting toward it and away.
Sohila's second hymn ends on that same observation, made long before anyone had a phone.

teach.h: A LIST OF TIME, TINY TO HUGE.
teach.b: The closing verse is a list of time, from tiny to huge. Visue and chasiaa: the smallest units of the old Indian clock, flickers of a moment. Gharhiaa: the ghari, a slice of the old Indian day.
Pahraa: the pahar, one of the watches the day and night were divided into. Thitee: the lunar days. Vaaree: the weekdays.
Maahu: the months. Every one of them, the verse says, comes into being.

teach.h: SOORAJ EKO: THE SUN IS ONE.
teach.b: Then the turn: sooraj eko rut anek. The sun is one; the seasons are many.

And the last line: Nanak, so many are the Creator's forms. That's the picture behind yesterday's six schools. Nobody calls summer false because winter is real, or makes Thursday compete with Saturday.
They're the one sun, seen at different angles.

teach.h: EVERY DAY IS THE SAME LIGHT.
teach.b: In the same way, the hymn says, the many forms are the play of one Creator. A day of bad news and a day of laughing until it hurts are, in the hymn's picture, lit by the same sun; neither falls outside the One.
Some Sikh teachers link this to hukam, the Creator's order running through everything, which came up early on the path. The seasons don't argue about who's in charge. They turn.
Winter doesn't apologize for not being summer; it takes its turn under the same light, and then hands the light on.

how: Sikhs recite this verse each night as the close of Kirtan Sohila's second hymn, and its image of one sun and many seasons is a common illustration in Sikh teaching about the one Creator and many forms.

p: a slice of the old Indian day

it says the seasons are many and the sun is one.

games.q: you've listed every unit of time, from a flicker to a season. how does the hymn finish?
o: the sun is one; the seasons are many.
the seasons are endless and have no source.
games.why: sooraj eko rut anek: one sun, many seasons, and so many are the Creator's forms.

practice: Look at what the light touches, a wall, a leaf, the floor by a window, the back of your hand, or, if it's night, a lamp. Notice that the light on the wall and the light on your hand come from one place.
Rest there for a few breaths, and if you pray, say Waheguru once, softly.

wordCard.voice: Many seasons. The close of Sohila's second hymn: seconds, hours, days, months and seasons are many, but the sun is one, and so many are the Creator's forms.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sooraj, the sun; in the hymn, the one source of every season.

carryVoice: Your line: one sun. Many hours, many seasons, the same light. Day four hundred twenty-six, done.
